# Digest C — Micah 2:1–13 & 3:1–12 (Nogalski, NICOT 2024)

**Source:** James D. Nogalski, *The Book of Micah* (NICOT, 2024)
**Slice:** `.cache/micah-reingest-2026-07-18/range_C_mic2-3.txt` (raw lines 2116–2833)
**Scope:** II Greed, Evil, Confrontation, Hope (2:1–13); III Judgment on Jerusalem’s Leadership (3:1–12)
**Extractor rules:** Faithfulness only; attribute to Nogalski; no live wiki edits.
**Locus formula:** Mic verse + raw line ≈ local line + 2115

---

## Claims

### C-C-01 — Three units in Mic 2 with shared theme
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1–13 overview; local ~1–2; raw ≈2116–2117
- **Quote:** “Micah 2 contains three units (2:1–5, 6–11, 12–13) that share a common theme, yet each part exhibits distinctive characteristics that distinguish it from the surrounding verses.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski divides Mic 2 into three units—land-oppression condemnation (2:1–5), prophetic dispute (2:6–11), and restoration hope (2:12–13)—united by theme but distinct in character.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-02 — Rhetorical purpose of 2:1–11: condemn king/wealthy land seizure
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1–11 overview; local ~2; raw ≈2117
- **Quote:** “The sequence of the first two units serves a rhetorical purpose of condemning the social oppression created by the king and the wealthy who are taking land from other Judeans.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:1–5 and 2:6–11 as condemning social oppression by king and wealthy who seize land from fellow Judeans.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-03 — Speaker/genre shifts deliberate in 2:1–5
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1–5; local ~4–5; raw ≈2119–2120
- **Quote:** “One must pay careful attention to the stylistically constructed rhetoric of the passage since the speaker, genre, and time frame of the actions constantly change… Together the two speeches pronounce imminent judgment while describing the horrific effects that the unjust will feel once Yahweh begins the actual punishment.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski treats alternation of first-/second-/third-person and Yahweh’s speech vs. future lamenter in 2:1–5 as deliberate poetic style announcing imminent judgment and its effects on the unjust.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-04 — 2:12–13 as post-587 hope, secondary to eighth-century prophet
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13 overview; local ~11–12; raw ≈2126–2127
- **Quote:** “This promise, it has often been argued, offers hope to those who have been removed from the land, and thus probably reflects life after the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE, long after the lifetime of the prophet or Hezekiah… scholars have long treated these verses as a later addition to the book designed to provide hope and to affirm Yahweh’s good intentions for Yahweh’s people.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reports and accepts the scholarly consensus that 2:12–13 is a later (post-587) addition offering restoration hope, not an original eighth-century speech of Micah or of Hezekiah’s reign.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-05 — 2:1–5, 6–11 late eighth-century; Hezekiah/Shephelah setting
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1–11 dating; local ~13–14; raw ≈2128–2129
- **Quote:** “The first two sections (2:1–5, 6–11) are routinely read against the backdrop of the late eighth century… the first unit (2:1–5) confronts and condemns one group of powerful Judeans who are seizing the land of their own countrymen, with at least the implicit, if not explicit, support of the king… Hezekiah’s attempt to buttress the defense of Jerusalem and Judah by fortifying the Shephelah and the fact that the prophet Micah came from the region in question (since he was born in Moresheth-Gath).”
- **Claim:** Nogalski situates 2:1–5 and 2:6–11 in the late eighth century against Hezekiah’s Shephelah fortification/centralization and Micah’s origin in Moresheth-Gath.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-06 — Judgment–hope vacillation as structural feature of Micah
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13 and book structure; local ~15–16; raw ≈2130–2131
- **Quote:** “most scholars see these verses as part of an exilic expansion to the book of Micah that helped to create the vacillation of judgment and hope that dominates the final form of the book. This alternation of judgment and hope seeks to reinforce the polarity of the prophetic message: the need for accountability of ethical and cultic expectations tempered with Yahweh’s grace and mercy toward those in Zion.”
- **Claim:** For Nogalski, 2:12–13 as exilic expansion helps produce the book’s characteristic judgment–hope alternation (also in chs. 4–5 and 6–7), balancing ethical/cultic accountability with Yahweh’s mercy.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-07 — Woe oracle form and round-the-clock scheming (2:1)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1; local ~58–59; raw ≈2173–2174
- **Quote:** “The opening word of 2:1, woe, evokes the somber tone of a funeral and immediately signals to the reader the judgmental rhetoric to follow… The schemes are hatched at night and executed by day (in the morning light), implying this evil does not stop. These people behave immorally but they appear to have some level of authorization to do what they do since the prophet implies that the motivation for their actions derives simply from their having the power to do what they want to do.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:1 as a woe oracle against a powerful group that plots at night, executes by day, and acts with impunity simply because it has power.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-08 — Group linked to Hezekiah’s centralizing reforms
- **Locus:** Mic 2:1; local ~61; raw ≈2176
- **Quote:** “scholars have speculated that the identity of the group in question must in some way be related to a politically powerful group, presumably even one related closely to the Judean monarchy. Furthermore, scholars suggest that the group to which this text alludes may have been those responsible for carrying out the reforms of Hezekiah that involved consolidating and centralizing the power of the king in Jerusalem.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reports scholarly identification of the 2:1 schemers with a politically powerful group, possibly agents of Hezekiah’s centralizing reforms.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-09 — Land seizure: fields, houses, household, inheritance (2:2)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:2; local ~62–63, 75; raw ≈2177–2178, 2190
- **Quote:** “Micah 2:2 contains two pairs of parallel versets describing the violent actions of those seizing property… and the consequences these actions have for the families affected… The loss of land does not merely mean the loss of a piece of property. Rather, it creates economic and social repercussions since that man and his family will lose all food production from the field, and that man will literally be unable to leave an inheritance to the next generation.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:2 as condemning violent seizure of fields and houses that oppresses man and household and destroys intergenerational inheritance (naḥălâ).
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-10 — ḥmd (“desire/covet”) and Decalogue echo
- **Locus:** Mic 2:2; local ~76; raw ≈2191
- **Quote:** “The verb “desire” here is the same root (ḥmd) typically translated as “covet” in the Decalogue (Exod 20:17), adding a powerful word that carries a heavy sense of taboo.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski notes that the land-grabbers’ “desire” uses the Decalogue root ḥmd (“covet”), intensifying the moral charge.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-11 — Judgment oracle: Yahweh “contemplating evil” on “this family” (2:3)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:3; local ~78–81; raw ≈2193–2196
- **Quote:** “Yahweh announces he is contemplating evil, thereby taking one element from each of the two opening accusations… In the context of the late eighth century BCE, this family taking the land from its owners with no legal repercussions would refer to the family of Hezekiah, the ruling monarch of Judah from 725–696 BCE.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads the 2:3 verdict (messenger formula + “therefore”) as poetic justice—Yahweh contemplates evil on “this family,” which he takes as an allusion to Hezekiah’s royal family confiscating Shephelah land for fortifications/taxes.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-12 — Yoke/haughtiness imagery in 2:3
- **Locus:** Mic 2:3; local ~82; raw ≈2197
- **Quote:** “The language in 2:3 implies that the punishment from Yahweh will serve as a yoke around the necks of its target… The arrogant will be humbled by being yoked to the service of another ruler.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski interprets 2:3’s neck/haughtiness language as yoke imagery: the arrogant will no longer walk high-headed, yoked under another’s rule.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-13 — 2:4–5 chronological extension; taunt/lament of reversed land allotment
- **Locus:** Mic 2:4–5; local ~84–90; raw ≈2199–2205
- **Quote:** “The second section of the judgment oracle (2:4–5) represents a chronological extension of 2:1–3… The opening of 2:4 announces that a taunt will come about in the form of a lamentation spoken by those who have been punished… He has changed the allotted portion of my people… so that the oppressor who has taken the houses and fields of others now finds himself in the situation where his own land has been taken.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski treats 2:4–5 as future extension of the verdict: a taunt/lament in which the former oppressor suffers reversed loss of allotted land (ḥēleq) under Yahweh’s judgment.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-14 — šôbēb ambiguity: “one returning” vs “apostate”
- **Locus:** Mic 2:4 text note / commentary; local ~55, 91; raw ≈2170, 2206
- **Quote:** “This last clause in the quoted speech remains ambiguous because the word šôbēb can be understood in two very distinct ways to mean “the one returning” or “an apostate.” Those opting for the former usually assume this verse represents a later setting from the early postexilic period… Others, including my translation, understand the form in a more positive sense, the “one who restores” or “returns.””
- **Claim:** Nogalski translates šôbēb positively as “the one returning/restoring” rather than “apostate,” while noting the postexilic-setting alternative.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-15 — No lot in Yahweh’s assembly; loss of land-ownership rights (2:5)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:5; local ~94–101; raw ≈2209–2216
- **Quote:** “To understand this verse, one must deduce from other contexts what it means to stretch a line … with a lot and how to identify the assembly of Yahweh… Sweeney sees the act of stretching a line as referring to a right of land ownership… the image of dividing land appears with the same verb in Amos 7:17… The family (i.e., clan) who is currently taking the land allotted to others will themselves lose their own allotted territory.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:5 as barring the guilty from land-allocation-by-lot in the assembly of Yahweh—loss of landowner rights—paralleling Amos 7:17 and Num/Josh allotment imagery; if aimed at the royal family, it implies danger for Jerusalem.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[amos]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-16 — 2:6–11 as prophetic disputation; early resistance to Micah
- **Locus:** Mic 2:6–11; local ~162–164; raw ≈2277–2279
- **Quote:** “Micah 2:6–11 takes on the form of a prophetic disputation. This disputation provides evidence of early resistance to the message of Micah… The intensity of the challenges and the counterclaims testifies to the strong investment by both sides… Since the imagery of the disputation concerns the content of speeches, the antagonists have regularly been identified as other prophets.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski classifies 2:6–11 as a prophetic disputation preserving confrontation with opponents (often identified as other prophets) who try to silence Micah.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-17 — nṭp “preach/drool”; opponents silence judgment (2:6)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:6; local ~165–170; raw ≈2280–2285
- **Quote:** “The verse begins with a prophetic statement telling a group not to preach (literally, “drip”) that which they are preaching… The prophetic speaker essentially characterizes their words as that which drools from their mouths… in its current location these things most naturally refer to the judgment pronouncements in 2:1–5. The prophet’s opponents attempt to silence him by claiming he does not speak for Yahweh… “He will not remove humiliations.””
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads triple nṭp in 2:6 as derogatory “preach/drool”: opponents tell Micah not to preach “these things” (the 2:1–5 judgments) and claim Yahweh will not remove humiliations—yet Nogalski takes the clause as affirming Yahweh’s intention to implement judgment.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[amos]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-18 — Rhetorical questions; words do good to the upright (2:7)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:7; local ~172–186; raw ≈2287–2301
- **Quote:** “The prophet’s counteroffensive begins with three rhetorical questions… Has the spirit of Yahweh become impatient? Yes… Are these Yahweh’s doings? Yes… Do my words not help the righteous? Yes… my words must refer to the prophet’s own words… The judgment announced there should serve as an admonition to change for anyone who considered themselves to be found among those who walk uprightly.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski assigns the 2:7 questions largely to the prophet: Yahweh’s spirit is impatient; these are Yahweh’s doings; Micah’s words (incl. 2:1–5) benefit those walking uprightly (yāšār), contrasting the haughty walk of 2:3.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-19 — Accusations: stripped travelers; expelled women/children (2:8–9)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:8–9; local ~190–200; raw ≈2305–2315
- **Quote:** “The prophet levels charges against the group of oppressors who have performed egregious acts of brutality and intimidation… the oppressors attacked the prophet’s people… robbed the clothes from people who should have had safe passage after fighting in a war… Micah 2:9 charges the oppressors with expelling women and children from their homes… When the prophet accuses the oppressors of removing Yahweh’s splendor from her children, it seems most likely that this idea relates well to the loss of inheritance that has already been cited (2:2, 4).”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:8–9 as charging oppressors with stripping travelers returning from war and driving women/children from homes, linking loss of Yahweh’s “splendor” (hādār) to loss of land-inheritance identity.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-20 — Verdict: leave unclean “resting place” (2:10)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:10; local ~202–211; raw ≈2317–2326
- **Quote:** “In 2:10, Yahweh commands the oppressors to leave because this is not the resting place… the verse functions better as a verdict than as a continuation of the accusations… Because it has become unclean, it will be destroyed, And the destruction will be grievous.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski prefers reading 2:10 as Yahweh’s verdict commanding oppressors to leave a defiled land/resting place that will be grievously destroyed, not merely a quotation of the oppressors’ eviction orders.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-21 — False prophet for wine and liquor (2:11)
- **Locus:** Mic 2:11; local ~212–215; raw ≈2327–2330
- **Quote:** “the prophet polemically quotes the words of a false prophet who offers to prophesy in return for payment. The sarcasm comes through loud and clear when the false prophet offers to preach, not for money, but for wine and liquor… No genuine prophet would say that Yahweh would condone the actions of the oppressors, so their message can only be classified as wind and falsehood… Micah 2:11 uses the same root (twice) that appeared in 2:6.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 2:11’s conditional as a sarcastic “mic-drop”: only a lying, wind-following preacher would sell messages for wine/liquor; the nṭp root returns the charge of 2:6 against false prophets.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-22 — 2:12–13: Yahweh gathers remnant; one speaker fluid first/third person
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13; local ~234–237; raw ≈2349–2352
- **Quote:** “The speaker of 2:12 must be Yahweh… 2:12–13 will be treated as a single speech unit… More likely, we should conceptualize the prophet speaking for Yahweh, though the prophet sometimes slips back into his own voice by referring to the deity in the third person.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski treats 2:12–13 as one unit with the prophet speaking for Yahweh, fluid between first-person divine speech and third-person reference to Yahweh.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-23 — Gathering as promise, not slaughter; king + Yahweh lead breakout
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13; local ~256–258; raw ≈2371–2373
- **Quote:** “in 2:12, Yahweh gathers the remnant of Israel. The presumption here is two-fold: Judgment has already occurred if there is a remnant, and the remnant has been scattered if they are now to be gathered… the action of 2:13 implies they are breaking out of the pen, led by their king and Yahweh. This last statement ultimately leads one to interpret 2:12–13 as a promise… the image of Yahweh at the head certainly seems better suited for consolation than condemnation.”
- **Claim:** Against minority judgment readings, Nogalski interprets the sheep-pen, breaker, king, and Yahweh-at-the-head imagery as promise of post-judgment restoration, not gathering for slaughter.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-24 — Parallel to Hos 1:11 and Amos 9:11; single king for Jacob/Israel
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13; local ~257–262; raw ≈2372–2377
- **Quote:** “Jacob/Israel is one entity and there is one king. This promise of a single king accompanying Yahweh aligns well with promises in Hosea and Amos that many believe also represent exilic updates… Hos 1:11 (2:2)… Amos 9:11 provides an even more explicit statement, indicating the restoration of David’s line.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski links Mic 2:12–13’s single king/Jacob-Israel unity to exilic-type restoration promises in Hos 1:11 and Amos 9:11.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[amos]], [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[remnant]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-25 — Why hope after 2:1–11: different enemies; exilic audience; carrot and stick
- **Locus:** Mic 2:12–13; local ~263–269; raw ≈2378–2384
- **Quote:** “In Mic 2:1–11, judgment largely focused upon inner Judean oppressors… Yet, Mic 2:12–13 presumes that the king and Yahweh fight on the same side… Scholars have long suggested that 2:12–13 represents an exilic or postexilic appropriation of Micah… This promise jumps forward to offer a word of hope to those who have experienced trauma and displacement at the hands of an enemy… The book of Micah, like Hosea, will structure its message as a series of warnings and promises, the carrot and the stick.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski explains 2:12–13 as exilic/postexilic hope for a displaced remnant, shifting from inner-Judean land-grabbers to foreign trauma; structurally, Micah alternates warning and promise like Hosea.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-26 — Ch. 3 structure: three subunits; inclusio of leaders; climax 3:12
- **Locus:** Mic 3 overview; local ~401–403; raw ≈2516–2518
- **Quote:** “The third chapter of Micah consists of three subunits ending with a climactic summary verdict against Jerusalem: Micah 3:1–4 contains the prophetic response that originally continued 2:6–11; 3:5–8 offers a judgment oracle that targets false prophets; and 3:9–12 contains another judgment oracle… Both the first part (3:1–4) and last part (3:9–12) address themselves specifically to the leaders of Jacob/Israel, providing an inclusio that unites the chapter… the identity of those creating the problem in Mic 3 as including both political and religious leadership.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski structures Mic 3 as three parts (leaders 3:1–4; false prophets 3:5–8; leaders/priests/prophets 3:9–12) framed by leader-inclusio, climaxing in Jerusalem’s destruction; political and religious leadership together are the problem.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-27 — 3:12 midpoint of Twelve; Jer 26:18 citation (overview)
- **Locus:** Mic 3:12 overview; local ~403; raw ≈2518
- **Quote:** “The Masoretic tradition marks 3:12 as the midpoint of the Book of the Twelve, providing evidence that the Twelve were copied as a single scroll. Relatedly, in the prophetic narratives of Jeremiah, the supporters of the prophet cite Mic 3:12 (see Jer 26:18) as authoritative evidence for why Jeremiah should not be put to death.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski notes MT tradition marking Mic 3:12 as midpoint of the Book of the Twelve (single-scroll evidence) and Jer 26:18’s citation of 3:12 to spare Jeremiah.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-28 — “And I said” continues 2:6–11, not 2:12–13
- **Locus:** Mic 3:1; local ~439; raw ≈2554
- **Quote:** “the opening word of 3:1 (wāʾōmar, meaning and I said) makes far less sense as a response to the promise than it does as the continuation of the disputation in 2:6–11. The end of 2:6–11 quoted the false prophets and the I speaking in 3:1 introduces the prophet’s own response to them.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski argues diachronically that 3:1’s “And I said” originally continues the 2:6–11 disputation, not the secondary hope of 2:12–13.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-C-29 — Rhetorical question on justice; dual sense of mišpāṭ (3:1)
- **Locus:** Mic 3:1, 4; local ~440–441; raw ≈2555–2556
- **Quote:** “Should you not know justice?… The Hebrew word translated justice (mišpāṭ)… has both a positive and a negative connotation… the description of the verdict in 3:4 causes one to realize that it is the leaders themselves who have petitioned Yahweh for justice without realizing that it is their own crimes that are now creating a scenario where justice means punishing those leaders.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 3:1’s justice question as accusation whose irony becomes clear in 3:4: leaders petition for justice while themselves being the ones justice will punish.
- **Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-C-30 — Cannibalistic leadership imagery (3:2–3)
- **Locus:** Mic 3:2–3; local ~447–451; raw ≈2562–2566
- **Quote:** “the third appositional clause… utilizes images of slaughtering and butchering of animals as a metaphor… accuses the leaders of mutilating their own bodies… 3:3 moves from describing the leaders’ self-mutilation (3:2b) to equating their actions with cannibalism… [those] who devour the flesh of my people, while the remainder of the verse graphically describes the cooking process. The animal is skinned, and then its bones are broken before it is chopped into pieces and thrown into the kettle.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski interprets 3:2–3’s butchery/cooking imagery as double metaphor: leaders mutilate their own body politic and cannibalize Yahweh’s people—not literal human sacrifice.

### C-C-34 — Verdict: night without vision; no divination (3:6–7)

### C-C-35 — Micah filled with strength, spirit, justice, might (3:8)
- **Locus:** Mic 3:8; local ~527–528; raw ≈2642–2643
- **Quote:** “the genuine prophetic character (Micah) contrasts his own power under the spirit of Yahweh with the impotence of the other prophets… I am filled with strength, justice, and might that come from the spirit of Yahweh… to declare to Jacob/Israel that it has done wrong… This purpose statement picks up the motifs from 1:5 (rebellion, sin, Israel, and Jacob).”
- **Claim:** Nogalski reads 3:8 as Micah’s self-contrast with false prophets: filled with strength, spirit of Yahweh, justice, and might to declare Jacob/Israel’s rebellion and sin, linking back to 1:5.

### C-C-36 — Mic 3 cumulatively condemns political and religious leadership for greed
- **Locus:** Mic 3 overview / 3:5–8; local ~498; raw ≈2613
- **Quote:** “Mic 3 cumulatively accuses the entire gamut of religious and political leadership of Judah for leading the people astray in order to better their own economic situation.”

- **Locus:** Mic 3:12; local ~599, 708–709; raw ≈2714, 2823–2824
- **Quote:** “Within the Book of the Twelve, the Masoretes marked this verse as the center point of the Book of the Twelve. The marginal notes of Codex Leningrad specify 3:12 as “The midpoint of the scroll.”… The Masoretic note at the end of Malachi correctly counts the number of verses in the Book of the Twelve as 1050, and reading from Hosea forward, Mic 3:12 is verse 525.”
- **Claim:** Nogalski documents Codex Leningrad’s mark of Mic 3:12 as midpoint of the Twelve scroll (verse 525 of 1050), not midpoint of Micah alone—evidence the Twelve were one scroll; he suspects the placement may not be accidental.
